newsitem.title: USA: Murdoch's Fox out to buy baseball's storied Dodgers.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's Fox out to buy baseball's storied Dodgers.

text.p: Media mogul Rupert Murdoch moved closer to owning one of America's most famous sports franchises Tuesday when the Los Angeles Dodgers sought permission to sell the baseball team to Fox Sports.

The sale, which reportedly could top $350 million, would set up an intriguing confrontation between Murdoch and his rival media mogul, CNN founder Ted Turner. Turner is vice chairman of Time Warner Inc., which owns the Atlanta Braves, a National League competitor of the Dodgers.
A Fox sale also would represent a major move into U.S. sports ownership by a company that has up until now only been involved in broadcasting sports, movies and television programs around the world.
Fox stunned the U.S. sports world by outbidding CBS in 1993 for the right to show some National Football League games.
The upstart network added insult to injury a few months later by snatching eight affiliated stations from CBS on the strength of its football broadcasts.

Under Murdoch, Fox has sought to expand its influence and compete with other entertainment giants such as Walt Disney Co. and Time Warner, both of which have been snatching up entertainment and sports assets in recent years.
Fox also has a deal with the National Hockey League and Major League Baseball to air games nationally.
Corporate ownership of baseball teams is a growing trend. Already the Tribune Co. owns the Chicago Cubs and Disney owns 25 percent of the Anaheim Angels.
In a statement, the Dodgers said the team was seeking permission from the league to enter into serious discussions with the Fox Group, an affiliate of News Corp.

Permission was expected to be granted by Major League Baseball's Executive Council for the talks to continue and the deal could be presented next month for league approval. It would require 75 percent approval by the other 27 team owners.

Fox, a unit of Murdoch's News Corp., had no comment on the proposed deal, which was worth a reported $350 million -- about twice the previous record of $173 million paid for the Baltimore Orioles in 1993.
If Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles and the club's spring training facilities at Dodger Town in Florida are included in the deal, it could top $400 million.

A source close to News Corp. confirmed the two sides were in talks, and said something should happen in the middle or end of next week. The Wall Street Journal, quoting sources familar with the negotiations, said O'Malley and Murdoch had already reached a tentative agreement.
The Dodgers, controlled since 1950 by the O'Malley family, said Fox was one of several groups that had expressed interest in the team.
"We're in the fifth month of what we expected to be a six-month process," said O'Malley, who shocked the sports world in January when he announced he was putting the Dodgers up for sale.

At the time, he said the era of family-owned sports franchises was over. O'Malley's father Walter broke millions of hearts in New York when he moved the Brooklyn Dodgers to Los Angeles for the 1958 season.
Under Peter O'Malley's presidency since 1970, the Dodgers have won two World Series titles, five National League pennants and finished first or second in their division 19 times.
And in an era of managerial revolving doors, the team has had only three managers -- Walter Alston, Tommy Lasorda and now Bill Russell.

It has also earned a reputation for developing new talent. The last five National League Rookies of the Year have been Dodgers -- Eric Karros, Mike Piazza, Raul Mondesi, Hideo Nomo and Todd Hollandsworth.
